History:
• Presenting complaint: Progressive shortness of breath.  
• Onset & course: Gradual worsening over ~2 weeks; markedly worse over the past few days. Now breathless walking short distances and inside the house.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild dry cough; new bilateral ankle swelling noted over the last few days; feels slightly run-down.  
• Denies: Chest pain, palpitations, fever/temperature, dizziness, orthopnea, PND.  
• Functional impact: Needs to sit and catch breath when walking to shops; concerned about ability to work as a part-time lorry driver.  
• Triggers/relievers: None specifically mentioned.  
• Previous similar episodes: Similar ankle swelling during prior heart-failure flare.

Past Medical History:
• Chronic heart failure (etiology: prior “small heart attack” ~5 yrs ago, probable MI).  
• Remote myocardial infarction (“small heart attack,” exact diagnosis name unknown).  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.  
• Medications:  
  – Furosemide (loop diuretic) — dose/route/frequency not documented; currently 1 tab daily, advised to increase to 1 tab twice daily.  
  – Aspirin — dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  – Bisoprolol — dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Allergies: Denies drug allergies.  
• Family history: Father died of myocardial infarction in early 60s; mother alive with osteoporosis.  
• Social history: Lives alone with two cats; part-time lorry driver (day shifts); ex-smoker (~1 pack/day for 25 yrs, quit); denies alcohol; limited exercise (daily walk to shops).

Physical Examination:
• General: Appears run-down but otherwise well (per clinician’s comment).  
• Cardiovascular/respiratory: Clinician states chest exam, oxygen saturations, and blood pressure “all OK.” No chest pain reported.  
• Extremities: Bilateral ankle swelling/oedema reported by patient.  
• Neurologic: Alert and oriented (implicit).  
• Other systems: No fever; no urinary changes other than baseline polyuria from diuretic use.  
• Vital signs: Not recorded.

Impression:
Likely acute decompensation of known congestive heart failure with volume overload (worsening dyspnea + new bilateral ankle oedema).  
Consistent differentials (per DDx and transcript):  
1. Acute decompensated heart failure – most consistent with history of HF and current fluid-overload signs.  
2. Viral/bacterial lower-respiratory infection precipitating HF flare – possible given cough/run-down feeling but no fever or abnormal lung exam.  
3. Pulmonary embolism – less likely; onset more gradual and no classic PE features.

Management Plan:
• Medication adjustment: Increase Furosemide from current regimen to 1 tablet twice daily for the next few days, then reassess (exact dose not documented).  
• Diagnostics ordered:  
  – Blood tests: CBC (rule out anemia/infection) and renal function/electrolytes.  
  – Echocardiogram to reassess cardiac function; to be scheduled within 1–2 weeks.  
• Follow-up: Review appointment in 1 week to evaluate symptom response and lab results.  
• Safety-net advice: If breathlessness worsens, or new chest pain, palpitations, or dizziness occur, instructed to call clinician sooner or seek urgent care.

Patient Summary:
Middle-aged man with known chronic heart failure presents with 2-week progressive dyspnea and new bilateral ankle oedema, consistent with a heart-failure exacerbation. Diuretic dose increased and labs/echo arranged; follow-up in one week.

Key Takeaways:
• Start taking Furosemide at the new higher frequency (1 tablet twice daily) starting today.  
• Monitor symptoms; seek immediate help for worsening breathlessness, chest pain, or dizziness.  
• Attend scheduled blood test and echocardiogram appointments.

Next Steps:
• Complete ordered blood work and echocardiogram.  
• Re-evaluate in one week; adjust therapy based on clinical response and test results.  
• Long-term: Continue HF guideline-directed medical therapy; reinforce lifestyle measures (smoking abstinence, moderate activity as tolerated).
